title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
oneLiner: Instead of trusting the model's memory, look up the relevant documents first and hand them to the model, so answers are current, private-data-aware and checkable.

what.html:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds a search step before the model answers. Documents are cut into chunks and indexed. For each question, a retriever finds the most relevant chunks (by meaning, by keywords, or both), an optional reranker puts the best first, and the model answers using only those chunks, with citations.

Everyday versionAn open-book exam. The student still has to understand and write the answer, but they look up the facts in their books and notes instead of relying on memory, and can point to the page they used.

why.html:
• It's the most common way companies use LLMs on their own documents.
  • It reduces made-up answers and adds sources.
  • Updating knowledge means editing documents, not retraining.

how.title: Why look things up?
how.html: The model's memory stops at its training date, never saw your private files, and can invent details. Fetching real text fixes all three.

how.title: Index, retrieve, augment, generate
how.html: Prepare documents once; then for every question fetch the top passages, paste them into the prompt, and generate an answer that cites them.

how.title: Search by meaning
how.html: Texts become arrows (vectors); similar meanings point the same way. Similarity is the cosine of the angle: (1, 2) and (2, 1) score 0.8.

how.title: Search by keywords, or both
how.html: Keyword search (BM25) nails exact codes like "E42"; meaning search catches "money back" ≈ "refund". Combining them catches both.

how.title: Cut documents well
how.html: Chunks too small lose context; too big get vague. Splitting by headings or overlapping chunks keeps facts in one piece.

how.title: Put the best first
how.html: Grab many candidates fast, then a more careful model reorders them so the truly relevant passage reaches the prompt.

how.title: Tables need queries
how.html: "Which city had the highest Q2 sales?" needs filtering and sorting, so the model writes a query, it runs, and the result (Chennai, 175) becomes the answer.

demo.html: Match each RAG problem to the component that fixes it.

example.html:
Cosine similarity. Query (1, 2), document (2, 1): dot product 1×2 + 2×1 = 4; lengths √5 each; 4 / 5 = 0.8. Fairly similar, but not the same direction.

Supplementary Even with very long context windows, retrieval still helps: stuffing in everything is slow and costly, and models use information buried in the middle of long prompts less reliably.

misunderstandings: RAG means the model learns the documents.
Nothing is trained; text is added to the prompt.
Vector search is always better than keywords.
Keywords win on exact codes and names.
A citation proves the answer is supported.
They dilute relevance and cost tokens.
takeaways: RAG = retrieve → augment → generate, with citations.
BM25 for exact terms; hybrid with RRF for both.
Chunk by structure or with overlap; rerank the top candidates.
Tables: text-to-SQL or code, not similarity search.
thirty: RAG supplements frozen, fuzzy parametric knowledge with retrieved non-parametric text at query time, giving current and private knowledge, citations and easy updates. Offline: chunk documents, embed and index them with metadata. Online: retrieve top-k, augment the prompt (answer only from context, cite, admit unknowns), generate. Dense retrieval uses bi-encoder embeddings and cosine similarity (q·d / |q||d|; (1,2) vs (2,1) = 0.8) with approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. BM25 scores exact terms with IDF, k₁ saturation and b length normalisation; hybrid fusion (reciprocal rank fusion, Σ 1/(60 + rank)) combines both. Chunking: fixed with overlap, structure-aware or semantic; a few hundred tokens typical. Reranking with cross-encoders re-orders top candidates for precision. Tables and semi-structured data need text-to-SQL or code execution (filter Q2, max sales → Chennai 175).

opts: Current and private knowledge with citations
